entry.title: Relative Energy Deficiency in Sport and its Implications for the Foot and Ankle Surgeon.
entry.content:
Wong C, Zide J, Alejandro S · Foot Ankle Clin · 2026

Relative energy deficiency in sport (RED-S) is a syndrome caused by low energy availability that affects multiple physiologic systems in both male and female athletes. Stress fractures of the foot and ankle are often the first signs of RED-S; therefore, it is crucial that orthopedic surgeons are aware of and able to identify this disorder. This article focuses on RED-S and provides a framework for understanding the disorder, it's relevancy to the orthopedic foot and ankle surgeon, and offers suggestions for diagnostic strategies and treatment approaches that are imperative for safe return to play.

entry.title: Test-Retest Reliability of Soft Tissue Vibration Variables Across an Outdoor 5-km Run.
entry.content:
Durante G, Jordan MJ, Pasanen K, Herzog W, et al. · J Appl Biomech · 2026

The purpose of this study was to determine the test-retest reliability of soft tissue vibration (STV) measurements taken superficial to the medial gastrocnemius during a 5-km outdoor run. Twenty-eight trained athlete participants (female: n = 14 and male: n = 14) wore a triaxial inertial measurement unit mounted on the skin superficial to their medial gastrocnemius (500 Hz) and performed two 5-km outdoor runs on different days at a controlled, individualized pace. STV outcome measures-peak acceleration, damping coefficient, settling time, peak and median frequency, and power-were analyzed using a continuous wavelet transform from averaged running strides within the entire run and among three 1500-m segments from each testing session. Intraclass correlation coefficients reinforced good to excellent between-day reliability measures (.75-.92) for all STV outcome measures except peak frequency (.50) and moderate to excellent reliability when comparing days across the 3 segments of the run (.70-.94), except for peak frequency (.44-.57). No significant day × time interactions were observed (P = .06-.63). Overall, STV outcome measures assessed with an inertial measurement unit during outdoor running demonstrated good reliability, supporting methodologies to quantify STV in real-world settings with potential applications in running performance and injury prevention research.

entry.title: [Design and analysis of a serial ankle rehabilitation robot].
entry.content:
Dai Y, Tao Q, Liu C, Li G, et al. · Sheng Wu Yi Xue Gong Cheng Xue Za Zhi · 2026

To address the complex mechanism configurations, strong motion coupling, and control complexity associated with some existing ankle rehabilitation robots, a two-degree-of-freedom serial ankle rehabilitation robot with independent actuation is proposed. The robot is capable of providing single-degree-of-freedom training in plantarflexion/dorsiflexion and adduction/abduction, as well as compound motion training. A kinematic model of the spatial orthogonal 2R mechanism was established, and its kinematic performance was analyzed. Ankle posture coupling constraints were introduced to refine the workspace. A prototype of the rehabilitation robot was subsequently fabricated, and ankle angle-tracking experiments were conducted using a Vicon three-dimensional motion capture system. The results showed that the mechanism had no singular configurations within the physiological range of motion of the human ankle. The maximum condition number was 1.414. In the prototype experiments, the mean absolute error and root mean square error for plantarflexion/dorsiflexion were 1.443° and 1.650°, respectively. For adduction/abduction, the corresponding values were 0.789° and 1.005°. These results demonstrate the feasibility of the proposed robot configuration for ankle rehabilitation and its favorable performance in tracking human ankle joint angles during robot-assisted motion.

entry.title: [Sensorimotor insoles for musculoskeletal disorders : An evidence-based rapid review].
entry.content:
Walther M, Greitemann B, Kerkoff A, Seeßle M, et al. · Orthopadie (Heidelb) · 2026

Sensorimotor foot orthoses (SMFOs) are designed to modulate afferent input through targeted plantar stimuli and thereby influence neuromuscular control mechanisms. This review aimed to provide an evidence-based assessment of their clinical effectiveness across different musculoskeletal conditions. We conducted a rapid review of randomized controlled trials and systematic reviews. We evaluated the available evidence for different orthotic concepts on an indication-specific basis using the GRADE approach. The strongest evidence was for symptomatic flexible pes planovalgus and patellofemoral pain syndrome, although no consistent superiority of SMFOs over conventional supportive foot orthoses was demonstrated. In patients with patellofemoral pain syndrome, randomized data showed significant improvements in pain and function with both SMFOs and conventional foot orthoses. For chronic ankle instability, the evidence regarding sensorimotor interventions is largely limited to mechanistic and indirect outcomes. Interpretation is further complicated because the textured insoles used in many studies do not match what is traditionally understood as SMFOs in German-speaking orthopedic practice. Evidence for SMFOs in nonspecific low back pain is even more limited and is characterized by heterogeneous findings. Based on the current literature, no clear superiority of sensorimotor orthotic concepts can be demonstrated for any specific diagnosis. However, this should not be interpreted as evidence of general ineffectiveness. SMFOs represent a therapeutic option within multimodal treatment strategies and should be prescribed according to the individual indication and patient-specific treatment goals.

entry.title: Cost Analysis and Clinical Outcomes of Staged Versus Single-Stage Fixation in the Management of Trimalleolar Ankle Fractures.
entry.content:
Mantı N, Daylak A, Akbulut AB, Memiş K, et al. · J Am Podiatr Med Assoc · 2026

Trimalleolar ankle fractures (TMFs) compromise ankle biomechanics; optimal operative strategy is debated. We compared single-stage open reduction and internal fixation (ORIF) with staged external fixation (EF) plus ORIF for outcomes and hospital billed charges. Retrospective cohort of adults treated 2018-2022 at a tertiary center. EF + ORIF (n = 40) vs. ORIF (n = 49). length of stay (LOS), hospital billed charges (stage-1, stage-2, total), readmission, additional surgical procedures, complications, and visual analog scale (VAS), American Orthopaedic Foot and Ankle Society (AOFAS), Short Form-36 (SF-36) to 2 years. After multivariable adjustment, ORIF was associated with a lower first-stage hospital billed charge (charge ratio, 0.55; 95% CI, 0.37-0.81; p = 0.003), a lower total hospital billed charge (charge ratio, 0.33; 95% CI, 0.24-0.47; p < 0.001), and earlier partial and full weight-bearing. Adjusted AOFAS scores were higher in the ORIF group at 3 months, 6 months, and 1 year, but not at 2 years. Holm-adjusted postoperative VAS contrasts were not significant, and the SF-36 group-by-time interaction was not significant. In this clinically selected cohort, single-stage ORIF was associated with lower hospital billed charges, earlier partial and full weight-bearing, and higher adjusted AOFAS scores at selected early follow-up points. Because Tscherne grade 2 and 3 injuries occurred only in the staged-treatment group, these findings do not establish comparative effectiveness for those injury grades or long-term functional superiority. Temporary external fixation remains an appropriate bridging strategy when soft-tissue conditions preclude immediate ORIF. Level III, retrospective cohort.

entry.title: Double-level osteotomy versus high tibial osteotomy for varus malalignment of the knee: A systematic review and meta-analysis.
entry.content:
Alkatheeri A, Ghandour M, Mobarak HA, Pierce T, et al. · Knee Surg Sports Traumatol Arthrosc · 2026

To compare double-level osteotomy (DLO) with high tibial osteotomy (HTO) for varus knee malalignment across patient-reported, radiographic, operative and complication outcomes. PubMed, Scopus and Web of Science were searched to 15 May 2026 for comparative DLO versus HTO studies. Outcomes were pooled with a random-effects model as mean differences (MD) or risk ratios (RR) with 95% confidence intervals (CI), with absolute values for each arm. The primary outcome was joint-line obliquity (JLO). Sensitivity analyses (leave-one-out, one cohort per centre, comparable indications) were post hoc. Nine observational studies (805 knees; 306 DLO, 499 HTO) were included. At a mean follow-up of 3 years, postoperative JLO was lower after DLO than after HTO (four studies; 1.6° vs. 5.9°; MD: -4.14°, 95%CI: -5.22, -3.06; I2 = 76%). DLO produced a lower MPTA (seven studies; 91.3° vs. 95.4°; MD: -4.10°, 95%CI: -5.30, -2.90), LDFA (four studies; 86.0° vs. 90.2°; MD: -4.04°, 95%CI: -4.49, -3.58) and mLDFA (two studies; 85.6° vs. 89.0°; MD: -3.37°, 95%CI: -4.16, -2.58). The hip-knee-ankle angle difference was small (five studies; MD: -0.96°, 95%CI: -1.83, -0.09) and not robust in sensitivity analyses. No difference was demonstrated for joint-line convergence angle, posterior tibial slope, any KOOS subscale, KSS scores or time to return to sport. Operative time was longer with DLO (two studies; 137 vs. 91 min; MD: 42.9, 95%CI: 25.7, 60.2). Intraoperative hinge fracture was less frequent with DLO (three studies; 14.0% vs. 34.6%; RR: 0.41, 95%CI: 0.23, 0.73). No nonunion was reported. At 3 years, no significant difference in patient-reported or functional outcomes was demonstrated between DLO and HTO. DLO achieved correction with less JLO and fewer hinge fractures, at the cost of a longer operation. Because DLO was often selected for bifocal or larger deformities, the radiographic differences partly reflect the indication. These hypothesis-generating findings require prospective confirmation. entry.title: Effects of sensorimotor training combined with short foot exercise on knee and ankle gait kinematics in individuals with flatfoot: A preliminary study.
entry.content:
Moon DC, Jung JH · Medicine (Baltimore) · 2026

Flatfoot, a common condition characterized by medial longitudinal arch collapse, alters foot and lower-limb mechanics. Sensorimotor training and short-foot exercises can improve postural stability and functional performance. However, their combined effects on gait kinematics remain unclear. This preliminary study evaluated the 6-week effects of combining these interventions on knee and ankle gait kinematics in individuals with flexible flatfeet. Thirty-two asymptomatic young adults with flexible flatfoot (14 males, 18 females; navicular drop ≥ 10 mm) were randomly assigned to an experimental group (sensorimotor training combined with short-foot exercises; n = 16) or a control group (sensorimotor training only; n = 16) using sealed opaque envelopes. Training was conducted 3 times per week for 6 weeks in a motion laboratory. Gait kinematics were assessed pre- and post-intervention using the VICON motion system. Outcomes included peak ankle inversion, eversion, dorsiflexion, and plantarflexion angles, knee internal and external rotation angles, and range of motion (ROM) in the sagittal, frontal, and transverse planes. Two-way repeated-measures analysis of variance was used for the analysis. The partial eta squared (ηp2) was reported as the effect size. Baseline demographics (age, sex, and body mass index) were similar between groups (P > .05). Significant group × time interactions were observed for gait variables. The experimental group showed a significant increase in peak ankle inversion (95% confidence interval (CI): 0.53-2.71; P = .004; ηp2 = 0.244) and a decrease in peak eversion (95% CI: 1.68-4.89; P = .002; ηp2 = 0.279). Peak knee internal rotation significantly decreased (95% CI: -9.92 to -2.82; P = .006; ηp2 = 0.228). Reductions were also observed in sagittal plane ankle ROM (95% CI: -4.88 to -0.68; P = .001; ηp2 = 0.317) and transverse plane knee ROM (95% CI: -7.75 to -4.01; P = .003; ηp2 = 0.254). No significant changes were found in ankle dorsiflexion, plantarflexion, knee external rotation, or frontal plane ankle ROM (P = .088, .126, .766, .136, respectively; ηp2 = 0.003-0.094). Combined sensorimotor and short-foot training more effectively improved gait kinematics than sensorimotor training alone, suggesting a promising non-surgical approach for managing flatfoot.

entry.title: Proof-of-Concept Evaluation of a Sock-Based Plantar Strain Sensing System for Diabetic Foot Monitoring.
entry.content:
Turnbull RP, Mason R, Sairally F, Corser J, et al. · Sensors (Basel) · 2026

Diabetic Foot Ulcers (DFUs) pose a serious health risk to people with diabetes, with a high risk of recurrence following the first DFU and a risk of foot amputation or death. It greatly impacts patient quality of life and costs the NHS up to 0.7% of its annual budget. Over the last 20 years, work has highlighted the link between DFU formation and normal forces. More recently, work has highlighted the importance of strain/shear forces, which are inherently coupled with normal forces. While limited lab-based in-shoe systems have been produced to detect shear, they alter the shoe-foot interface and are not commercially available. Additionally, consultation with people with diabetes highlighted that they may not wear shoes around the house, leaving long periods where in-shoe solutions cannot track forces. We, therefore, present the development of a novel plantar shear measuring system, the Shear Tracking for Enhanced Prevention Sock (STEPS), an instrumented garment to provide an accessible tool for people at risk of DFUs. Integrating sensors within the sock provides a solution that seamlessly integrates within the foot-shoe environment, is suitable for shoeless use, and helps mitigate adherence issues. A prototype STEPS was produced, successfully integrating printed resistive strain sensors (proxy for shear) within custom-designed socks with flexible connectivity to a welt-mounted data acquisition unit. Proof-of-concept testing characterised the system's ability to measure plantar strain. A single-participant pilot study demonstrated that STEPS captures repeatable, gait-synchronised strain signals during walking, with a stationary noise floor below 10% of the typical per-cycle resistance response and between-repeat correlations of R = 0.41 and 0.78 for Sensor 1 and 2 respectively, supporting its potential to detect strain (as proxy for shear) during daily activity.

entry.title: Smartphone-derived mobility metrics identify distinct recovery phenotypes following ACL reconstruction: associations with function, pain, and psychological health.
entry.content:
Kandakurti PK, Koura GM, Reddy RS, Kardm S, et al. · Knee Surg Relat Res · 2026

Recovery after anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) reconstruction is typically monitored through patient-reported outcomes and periodic clinical assessments, which may not fully capture real-world functional performance. Smartphone-derived mobility data provide a passive and objective approach for evaluating daily activity and recovery. To examine associations between smartphone-derived mobility metrics and recovery outcomes in adults 3-12 months after primary ACL reconstruction and to identify distinct recovery phenotypes using mobility-based clustering. This cross-sectional study included 120 adults who were 3-12 months post-primary ACL reconstruction and had at least 14 days of retrospective smartphone mobility data. Mobility variables included daily step count, activity volume and intensity (e.g., active minutes and walking bout duration), sedentary behavior, and walking-related metrics. Outcomes included pain (Numeric Rating Scale [NRS]), functional status (Knee Injury and Osteoarthritis Outcome Score [KOOS] Pain, Activities of Daily Living, and Sport/Recreation subscales), knee-related quality of life (ACL Quality of Life questionnaire [ACL-QoL]), and psychological measures including the Pain Catastrophizing Scale (PCS), Patient Health Questionnaire-9 (PHQ-9), and Generalized Anxiety Disorder-7 (GAD-7). Associations were evaluated using Pearson correlation and multivariable linear regression analyses. Recovery phenotypes were identified using unsupervised k-means clustering of mobility metrics. Higher daily step counts were independently associated with better KOOS-ADL scores (β = 0.48, p < 0.001), higher ACL-QoL scores (β = 0.45, p < 0.001), and lower pain intensity (β = - 0.39, p = 0.001). Three recovery phenotypes emerged: a high-activity/low-pain phenotype with superior function and minimal psychological distress, a moderate-activity/moderate-pain phenotype with intermediate outcomes, and a low-activity/high-pain phenotype characterized by reduced mobility, poorer function, greater pain, and higher pain catastrophizing. Significant gradients were observed across phenotypes for pain (NRS: 1.72-5.01), function (KOOS-Pain: 88.94-62.37), and pain catastrophizing (PCS: 8.52-24.91; all p < 0.001). Smartphone-derived mobility metrics were significantly associated with recovery outcomes following ACL reconstruction. Mobility-based clustering identified distinct recovery phenotypes associated with meaningful differences in pain, function, and pain catastrophizing, highlighting the potential of passive mobility monitoring to support personalized rehabilitation strategies. However, given the variability in evaluation periods and uncontrolled surgical factors, future research employing standardized, long-term follow-ups is warranted.

entry.title: The Impact of Hyperarch Fascia Training on Perceived Ankle Instability and Vertical Jump Performance in Physically Active Men and Women.
entry.content:
Hawkins KB, Xie C, Matias CA, Sikorski EM, et al. · Sports (Basel) · 2026

Chronic ankle instability (CAI) is a prevalent musculoskeletal condition that impairs physical performance and increases reinjury risk; yet, training programs emphasizing fascia-targeted techniques remain an understudied rehabilitation strategy. The purpose of this study was to examine the effects of 12 weeks of a multicomponent training intervention emphasizing fascia-targeted techniques (Hyperarch Fascia Training (HFT)) on perceived ankle instability and function, and vertical jump performance in individuals with CAI. In this decentralized, randomized controlled trial, 66 participants were randomized (HFT n = 44, CON n = 22), with 43 participants completing the study and being analyzed (HFT n = 22; CON n = 21). Selected subjects confirmed perceived ankle instability (CAIT score ≤ 25) and were assigned to either a structured, multicomponent HFT program with various foot and ankle strengthening exercises, or a passive control condition instructed to maintain activities of daily living. The HFT group experienced disproportionately higher attrition (n = 22 excluded from analysis) than CON (n = 1 excluded from analysis due to becoming unresponsive). The reasons for attrition in the HFT group were due to becoming unresponsive (n = 13), self-reported difficulty with the protocol (n = 3), scheduling conflicts (n = 3), or adverse events (n = 3, reported as moderate). Outcomes were assessed at baseline, week 8, and week 12 using the Cumberland Ankle Instability Tool (CAIT) (primary outcome), Foot and Ankle Ability Measure (FAAM) (primary outcome), countermovement jump (CMJ) (secondary outcome), and Short Form Health Survey 12 (SF-12) (exploratory outcome). The HFT group demonstrated significantly greater improvements in CAIT scores compared to CON (group × time interaction p = 0.008), with large within-group effect sizes in the HFT group relative to baseline (d = 1.49 and 1.54, at weeks 8 and 12, respectively). Significant group × time interactions also favored HFT for CMJ jump height (p = 0.017) and flight time (p = 0.005) (co-secondary outcomes), as well as the CMJ algorithmic derivatives of mean velocity (p = 0.001) and take-off velocity (p = 0.008) (exploratory outcomes). No significant group × time interactions were observed for FAAM ADL or Sport subscales. Significant group × time interactions were found for SF-12 survey results for Physical Function (p = 0.045), Limits due to Physical Health (p = 0.030) and General Health (p = 0.043), with CON tending to decline over time and HFT tending to improve. The HFT group was higher than CON on Physical Function at Week 8 (d = 1.04, p = 0.009), and on Perceived Pain at Week 12 (d = 0.88, p = 0.047). Overall, these findings suggest that a multicomponent fascia-centered training program may represent a viable intervention for improving perceived ankle stability and increasing the explosive vertical jump performance in individuals with CAI.

entry.title: Toward Wearable Joint Load Monitoring: Concurrent Estimation of Hip, Knee, and Ankle Sagittal Contact Forces from Sparse IMU Measurements.
entry.content:
Ma T, Fan X, Yu N, Han J, et al. · IEEE Trans Biomed Eng · 2026

Continuous monitoring of lower extremity joint contact forces is critical for rehabilitation medicine, sports injury prevention, and assistive device development. Yet, current wearable solutions often lack multi-joint integration or require cumbersome sensor arrays. This study aims to concurrently estimate hip, knee, and ankle sagittal compressive contact forces using a sparse inertial measurement unit (IMU) configuration across diverse daily activities. We collected data from 14 healthy adults equipped with four IMU sensors performing various daily movements, with reference contact forces captured using optical motion capture and force platforms. To estimate joint contact forces, we developed a domain-informed multi-task temporal convolutional network (Ada-Att-MTCN). This architecture integrates a shared temporal convolutional network encoder, task-specific attention mechanisms, homoscedastic uncertainty-based dynamic task weighting, and a soft physiological-bound penalty. Performance was evaluated using 14-fold leave-one-subject-out nested cross-validation against 4 baseline methods, with root mean square error (RMSE) and coefficient of determination (R²) as evaluation metrics. On the self-collected dataset, Ada-Att-MTCN achieved the highest accuracy across all activities, with mean RMSEs of 0.328 ± 0.13 BW (hip), 0.380 ± 0.09 BW (knee), and 0.365 ± 0.15 BW (ankle), and an average R2 of 0.822 ± 0.10. On the external dataset, Ada-Att-MTCN likewise performed best among all methods (average R² = 0.754 ± 0.05). The proposed framework captures complex inter-joint dynamics, enabling robust simultaneous load estimation with drastically reduced hardware complexity. This approach provides a practical, non-invasive solution for transitioning lab-grade multi-joint load monitoring to wearable deployment in rehabilitation and sports medicine.

entry.title: Tracking Recovery After TKA with Instrumented Timed Up and Go: Spatiotemporal, Rotational, and Strength Adaptations over Six Months.
entry.content:
Gianzina E, Yiannakopoulos CK, Bourantanis A, Armenis E, et al. · Sensors (Basel) · 2026

Knee osteoarthritis (KOA) is a leading cause of disability, and total knee arthroplasty (TKA) improves pain and functional mobility, although gait impairments may persist postoperatively. This study investigated longitudinal changes in patient-reported outcomes, muscle strength, and gait performance using an instrumented Timed Up and Go (iTUG) test with wearable inertial measurement units (IMUs). Twenty-two patients with end-stage KOA were assessed preoperatively and at 3, 12, and 24 weeks postoperatively. The Knee Injury and Osteoarthritis Outcome Score five-subscale composite (KOOS5) showed a significant overall change over time (p < 0.001), while isometric muscle strength showed significant overall changes across all tested muscle groups (p ≤ 0.008), with mean values demonstrating an initial postoperative decline followed by subsequent increases. Total TUG duration showed a significant overall time effect (p = 0.023), with significant reductions observed in the forward and return gait phases (p = 0.012 and p = 0.001, respectively). End-turning maximum rotational speed and sit-to-stand vertical acceleration showed significant overall time effects (p = 0.012 and p = 0.024, respectively), whereas the remaining parameters did not reach statistical significance. These findings indicate that recovery following TKA is multidimensional, with significant changes in patient-reported outcomes, muscle strength, and functional mobility. iTUG analysis identified phase-specific changes, while several turning and transitional parameters did not show significant longitudinal changes, supporting the use of targeted rehabilitation strategies focusing on dynamic stability and movement control.

entry.title: Effects of the FIFA 11 + neuromuscular warm-up program on Move2Perform injury risk classification in youth amateur soccer players: a randomized controlled trial.
entry.content:
Atabaş EG, Yapıcı A, Bağış YE · BMC Sports Sci Med Rehabil · 2026

Lower extremity injuries are a major concern in youth soccer, where multifactorial risk factors interact and isolated screening tools have demonstrated limited predictive accuracy. Neuromuscular warm-up programs such as the FIFA 11 + have shown efficacy in reducing injury incidence, yet limited evidence exists on their effect when combined with multifactorial risk-classification frameworks in amateur youth populations. The present study aimed to evaluate the effects of an eight-week FIFA 11 + neuromuscular warm-up program on injury risk profiles-classified by the Move2Perform algorithm-and on functional performance and injury incidence in youth amateur male soccer players. In this parallel-group, single-blinded randomized controlled trial, 44 male amateur soccer players aged 15-18 years competing in a regional amateur league were randomly allocated, using computer-generated block randomization, to an experimental group (n = 22) or a control group (n = 22). Injury risk was classified using the Move2Perform algorithm, which integrates demographic data, injury history, the Functional Movement Screen (FMS), and the Lower Quarter Y-Balance Test (YBT-LQ). Additional outcomes included jump performance and isometric quadriceps and hamstring strength. The experimental group performed the FIFA 11 + program three times per week for eight weeks under the supervision of a certified physiotherapist, while the control group continued their routine warm-up. Time-loss injuries were recorded prospectively during the eight-week period. A mixed-design ANOVA was used to assess Group × Time interactions. The experimental group showed significant improvements in YBT-LQ composite scores, FMS total scores, jump test performance, and quadriceps strength (p < 0.05), with significant Group × Time interactions favoring the FIFA 11 + group. Move2Perform risk classification shifted favorably in the experimental group: athletes initially categorized as Moderate Risk showed the most pronounced improvement, transitioning to Slight Risk, and three athletes initially classified as Substantial Risk moved to the Slight Risk category (descriptively notable, but not reaching statistical significance for this subgroup). The experimental group experienced significantly fewer time-loss injuries (n = 2) than the control group (n = 8) over the eight-week period (p = 0.009), with significantly lower incidences of ankle sprains (p = 0.038) and hamstring strains (p = 0.041). Athletes classified as high risk by the Move2Perform algorithm sustained approximately a threefold increase in injury occurrence compared with their lower-risk counterparts. An eight-week, supervised FIFA 11 + neuromuscular warm-up program produced favorable shifts in Move2Perform injury risk classification and reduced time-loss injury incidence in youth amateur soccer players. Combining multifactorial injury risk classification with structured neuromuscular warm-up appears to be a practical and effective strategy for reducing lower extremity injury risk in this population, supporting the integration of preseason group-based prevention with individualized corrective approaches. entry.title: Multimodal Gait Acquisition and Musculoskeletal Simulation for Subject-Specific Evaluation of Ankle Exosuit Cable Anchor Positioning in Cerebral Palsy.
entry.content:
Bermejo-García J, Martín-Fraile A, Ojeda J, Agujetas R, et al. · Biomimetics (Basel) · 2026

Wearable ankle exosuits require precise evaluation frameworks to optimize assistive force transmission and subject-specific configuration. This study presents a multimodal sensor-based experimental and computational framework to assess the influence of ankle exosuit cable anchor positioning on neuromuscular and energetic responses during gait in a child with spastic hemiplegic cerebral palsy. Three-dimensional kinematics were acquired using an optical motion capture system (12 infrared cameras), while ground reaction forces were recorded through instrumented force plates. Metabolic cost was experimentally measured using portable respiratory gas analysis. These sensor-derived data were integrated into a participant-scaled musculoskeletal model in OpenSim to simulate nine cable anchor configurations and quantify changes in muscle activation, force production, mechanical impulse, and metabolic power. Cable geometry altered the predicted distribution of plantar-flexor loading across configurations. Experimental measurements were not available for muscle-level outputs or for the assisted configurations; therefore, these responses were interpreted as model-derived, exploratory comparisons rather than experimentally validated physiological effects. Configurations with larger offsets from the heel-reference position tended to yield greater reductions in gastrocnemius demand, whereas configurations nearer the heel reference more effectively reduced soleus loading but increased secondary stabilizing muscle recruitment. Predicted metabolic changes across assisted configurations ranged from a 0.86% reduction to a 6.28% increase relative to the experimental baseline, and from a 2.66% reduction to a 4.33% increase relative to the simulated non-actuated condition. These differences should be interpreted as indicators of model sensitivity rather than demonstrated energetic improvements. This study demonstrates how multimodal gait sensing combined with musculoskeletal simulation provides a quantitative tool for preliminary screening of cable-driven ankle exosuit design in pathological gait.

Wang X, Shao X, Shi X, Adams RD, et al. · J Sport Rehabil · 2026

Up to 75% of lateral ankle sprain cases experience long-term impairments and suffer chronic ankle instability (CAI), a condition characterized by impaired ankle proprioception. This study aims to investigate ankle proprioceptive performance during functional tasks with increasing movement control and ankle joint load in individuals with and without CAI. Cross-sectional study. Twenty individuals with CAI and 19 healthy controls completed 4 proprioceptive tasks: standing, walking, landing (double-leg drop), and stair descent. In each task, their ability to discriminate between 4 ankle inversion angles was assessed using a task-specific discrimination apparatus. CAI participants had significantly lower ankle proprioception scores than controls (mean difference = 0.047, 95% CI, 0.031-0.063). Proprioceptive acuity varied by task (P < .001, ηp2=.345), with no significant group-by-task interaction (P = .220, ηp2=.039). Trend analysis showed a linear improvement in proprioceptive performance with increasing ankle load and challenge in controls (P < .001, ηp2=.685), whereas the CAI group showed both significant linear (P < .001, ηp2=.445) and quadratic (P = .001, ηp2=.430) trends, reflecting a rise followed by a significant downturn as load peaked. Both groups improved with greater load, but during stair descent, individuals with CAI exhibited a significant decline. This suggests that proprioceptive processing in CAI is impaired and may be overloaded during highly challenging tasks.

entry.title: Gait speed and multi-segment foot joint kinematics throughout the entire stance phase using statistical parametric mapping.
entry.content:
Jeong H, Hamill J, Boyer KA, van Emmerik REA · PeerJ · 2026

The foot is a multi-segment structure whose segments function together. Due to its ongoing connection with the support surface, the foot must be capable of managing loads that vary with gait speed. Previous studies have provided considerable insight into the relationship between foot joint kinematics and gait speed. However, their primary reliance on discrete measures, such as peak joint angles, has limited understanding of how these relationships evolve throughout the stance phase. The aim of this study was to investigate the effects of gait speed on full time-series trajectories of multiplanar foot joint kinematics using statistical parametric mapping. According to our findings, faster walking primarily increased ankle eversion and midfoot dorsiflexion during weight acceptance (∼17-29% of the stance phase). In contrast, during propulsion, faster walking increased ankle plantar flexion (∼80-100% of the stance phase) and inversion (∼82-90%), as well as midfoot plantar flexion (∼82-100%) and adduction (∼90-98%), together with greater dorsiflexion of the first metatarsophalangeal joint after heel-off (∼43-98% of the stance phase). These multiplanar joint kinematic alterations across the ankle-foot joints throughout the stance phase reflect greater foot-arch collapse in early stance and foot-arch recoil in late stance, which may facilitate appropriate energy absorption and generation in response to increasing gait speed. Posttraumatic arthrofibrosis is a rare cause of painful motion loss after injury or surgery, with limited available evidence. Reported rates range from 2% to 10% after ankle injuries to up to 73% after surgically treated fractures, while ankle-specific data on risk factors remain limited. Posttraumatic arthrofibrosis of the ankle is rare, underdiagnosed, and treatable. Modern sports science is undergoing a paradigm shift from subjective coaching to objective, data-driven precision training. Consequently, wearable electronics for acquiring precise data during sports activities are attracting attention. However, conventional rigid wearables inherently suffer from mechanical mismatches between rigid wearables and the soft, deformable human skin, inducing severe motion artifacts and restricting natural biomechanics during high-intensity athletic activities. To address these limitations from a comprehensive perspective, this review systematically summarizes and analyzes recent advancements in next-generation flexible and stretchable bioelectronics tailored specifically for sports applications. We systematically examine the substrate materials, structural engineering designs, and device-level optimization strategies required to withstand repetitive strain, shear, and sweat-intensive environments. Building upon these conformable bio-interfaces, we discuss three core sensing modalities: electrochemical sensors for real-time analysis of sweat biomarkers, biophysical sensors for continuous electrophysiological and hemodynamic monitoring, and electromechanical sensors for high-fidelity kinematic and impact tracking. Furthermore, we discuss body-derived energy harvesting strategies to power sports wearables and wireless communication systems for continuous athletic monitoring. The importance of artificial intelligence and machine learning is increasing, as these techniques enable the removal of motion artifacts and facilitate objective analysis of athletic data for training and health monitoring applications. By evaluating targeted applications across aerobic and anaerobic exercise, cognitive state assessment, and post-exercise recovery, this review demonstrates how next-generation sports wearables contribute to the shift in sports science from reactive treatment toward proactive, data-driven performance enhancement and injury prevention.

entry.title: Menstrual Cycle Phase-Dependent Lower Extremity Loading Patterns in Adolescent Female Athletes: Implications for Anterior Cruciate Ligament Injury Risk.

category.label: Menstrual cycle / hormonal phase & injury risk (sports)

entry.content:
Ulman S, Garcia J, Jones J, Davis A, et al. · J Pediatr Soc North Am · 2026

Physically active females experience substantially higher anterior cruciate ligament injury rates than males, and postmenarche adolescent females commonly demonstrate high-risk mechanics. However, whether mechanics fluctuate across the menstrual cycle remains poorly understood in adolescent female athletes. The aim of this study was to examine differences in lower extremity kinematics and kinetics across two menstrual cycle phases (menstruation and mid-luteal) in postmenarchal adolescent female athletes during a dynamic change-of-direction task. It was hypothesized that biomechanical contributors to dynamic knee valgus would differ between phases. A controlled laboratory study was conducted. Thirty healthy postmenarchal adolescent female athletes (aged 13-17 years) were tested during menstruation (verified by self-reported active bleeding) and mid-luteal phase (scheduled via calendar-based day counting). Kinematics and kinetics were collected using 3-dimensional motion capture and force plates while participants performed a 45° run-cut task. Peak pelvis, hip, and knee angles and hip and knee moments were extracted during the loading phase for each limb. Linear mixed-effects models tested effects of phase and limb dominance (α = 0.05). Participants were aged 15.6 ± 0.9 years, had a height of 168.8 ± 6.2 cm, and weighed 61.2 ± 7.0 kg, and a majority played soccer (70.0%). Compared with menstruation, the mid-luteal phase demonstrated greater peak anterior pelvic tilt (P = .018) and pelvic rise (P = .038), along with reduced peak knee flexion (P = .009). During menstruation, athletes exhibited greater hip abduction moment (P = .037), hip internal rotation moment (P = .043), knee valgus moment (P = .012), and knee external rotation moment (P = .007). Limb dominance effects were observed for pelvic rise (P < .001) and hip internal rotation moment (P = .047). Biomechanical contributors linked to dynamic knee valgus differed by menstrual cycle phase in adolescent female athletes during a change-of-direction task. Menstruation was associated with greater coronal- and transverse-plane hip and knee loading, whereas mid-luteal phase was associated with reduced knee flexion and greater pelvic instability. Cycle-synced injury prevention strategies that are individualized and evidence-based may enhance lower extremity stability when knee control appears most challenged. However, while cycle-synced training may not be feasible in all settings, awareness of phase-related vulnerability may inform screening and load management. To describe the longitudinal evolution of the Cumberland Ankle Instability Tool (CAIT) after arthroscopic anatomic lateral ligament reconstruction (AALR) and examine associations between CAIT-defined patient-perceived stability, return to sport (RTS) and preoperative factors. This retrospective single-centre cohort included 134 athletic patients who underwent AALR between January 2019 and January 2023 and had at least 12 months of follow-up. CAIT was assessed preoperatively and at 3, 6 and 12 months. Patient-perceived stability was defined as CAIT ≥ 24. Repeated continuous and binary outcomes were assessed using paired-data methods. RTS was defined as self-reported resumption of sport by 12 months, irrespective of level. Median CAIT increased from 8 preoperatively to 23, 26 and 28 at 3, 6 and 12 months, respectively (overall p < 0.001). CAIT-defined stability increased from 5/134 (3.7%) preoperatively to 55/134 (41.0%), 91/134 (67.9%) and 96/134 (71.6%) at 3, 6 and 12 months (overall p < 0.001). Most improvement occurred by 6 months. Overall, 112 patients (83.6%) reported RTS by 12 months. Higher CAIT at 3, 6 and 12 months was associated with RTS. In exploratory multivariable analysis, preoperative ankle ligament reconstruction-return to sport after injury was positively associated with 12-month CAIT-defined stability (odds ratio [OR]: 1.02, 95% confidence interval [CI]: 1.00-1.04; p = 0.043), whereas nonpivot sport was negatively associated compared with pivot-contact sport (OR: 0.27, 95% CI: 0.09-0.75; p = 0.014). Four patients (3.0%) underwent fibular button removal. entry.title: Calf Injuries: Anatomy, Pathology, and Treatment.
entry.content:
Hauer TM, Arner JW, Mauro CS, Bradley JP · J Am Acad Orthop Surg · 2026

Calf injuries are common in athletes and typically result in missed time from sport and activities of daily living. The three individual triceps surae muscles can be injured, with differing described mechanisms. Gastrocnemius or plantaris strains tend to occur during sudden explosive movement of the ankle from a dorsiflexed to a plantarflexed position with the knee in extension. Soleus strains typically occur from repetitive dorsiflexion of the ankle with the knee flexed. Imaging modalities such as magnetic resonance imaging and ultrasonography can be helpful in determining the location and grade of injury, which can aid in treatment and return to play timelines. Classically, these injuries have been graded as grade I, II, or III, with grade I having <10% muscle fiber disruption, grade II having >10 to 50% muscle fiber disruption, and grade III having 50 to 100% muscle fiber disruption. The mainstay of treatment for most calf strains is nonsurgical, with surgical management being rare but reported in the literature for isolated grade III ruptures of the medial head of the gastrocnemius. Return to sport and activities requires a graduated physical therapy program focused on restoring tissue length without excessive strain. Recent limited evidence has shown promising results with quicker return to activities and decreased pain with platelet-rich plasma injections.

entry.title: A Focused Narrative Review of Selected Evidence on Gymnastics Training Optimization, Technology, Athlete Health, and Injury Prevention.
entry.content:
Zaharie N, Neagu SG, Badescu D, Grosu VT, et al. · Healthcare (Basel) · 2026

Background: Sustainable gymnastics training requires a balance between performance development, injury prevention, workload management, athlete health, psychological well-being, and long-term participation. This focused narrative review aimed to synthesize selected evidence on training optimization, technological applications, athlete health and injury prevention in gymnastics. Methods: A structured narrative review was conducted using the Web of Science Core Collection. The literature search covered publications issued between 1 January 2005 and 30 September 2025, with the final search performed on 30 September 2025. English-language publications retrieved through three predefined Topic searches in the Web of Science Core Collection were considered. The searches covered the period from 1 January 2005 to 30 September 2025 and were restricted to the Sport Sciences category. No additional publications were identified through reference-list screening. Three complementary thematic searches addressing gymnastics training models, technological applications, and injury prevention identified 485 records. After applying the eligibility criteria, removing duplicates, assessing full texts, and excluding ineligible or retracted publications, 140 publications were included in the narrative synthesis. No formal risk-of-bias assessment was performed. Results: The reviewed evidence emphasized progressive and individualized training, workload monitoring, recovery, physical preparation, age-appropriate development, and early identification of pain, fatigue, and other health-related concerns. Injury occurrence was associated with biomechanical loading, rapid growth, training exposure, previous injuries, insufficient recovery, menstrual dysfunction, psychological factors, and discipline-specific technical demands. Wearable sensors, video analysis, biomechanical modelling, artificial intelligence, virtual reality, and digital learning platforms supported movement assessment, technical feedback, training monitoring, and education. Evidence for several emerging technological applications, particularly artificial intelligence and automated assessment, remains preliminary and requires further validation in gymnastics-specific and real-world settings. However, substantial differences in study designs, populations, technologies, outcome measures, and methodological characteristics limited direct comparison across studies. Coaching communication, athlete motivation, psychological well-being, and access to validated technologies also influenced the sustainability of gymnastics training. Conclusions: Sustainable gymnastics training may benefit from an interdisciplinary and athlete-centered approach integrating individualized load management, injury prevention, health monitoring, recovery, educational coaching practices, and appropriately validated technologies. The evidence identified in this review highlights converging themes suggesting the potential value of combining these components to support safe performance development and long-term participation. However, more longitudinal, discipline-specific, and methodologically consistent research is needed.

Davis Iv JJ, Meardon SA, Raglin JS, Brown AW, et al. · Med Sci Sports Exerc · 2026

Inexpensive consumer-grade wearable sensors have expanded possibilities to assess, monitor, or modify a runner's gait. However, it is unclear which sensor-measured gait metrics are strongly associated with internal loading at common injury locations. To measure the association between gait metrics measured by consumer-grade wearable sensors and internal forces at the Achilles tendon and the patellofemoral joint. 55 healthy runners wearing consumer-grade chest straps foot-pods completed a 38-minute run on an instrumented treadmill at 12 speeds from 70%-125% of self-reported typical running pace. A scaled musculoskeletal model derived from motion capture data and driven by static optimization was used to calculate Achilles tendon and patellofemoral joint forces during stance for each speed. Functional regression models were used to estimate the associations of each of nine sensor-measured gait metrics with internal forces across stance, after adjusting for body mass and running speed. At both the Achilles tendon and the patellofemoral joint, cadence, vertical oscillation, and vertical ratio (vertical oscillation divided by step length) showed the strongest associations with internal forces (maximum of 0.4-0.6 BW change in force per one standard deviation change in the gait metric). Other wearable sensor-measured gait metrics, including stance time, leg stiffness, and stance time percent showed weaker associations (<0.4 BW change in force per one standard deviation change in the gait metric). Runners with higher-than-average cadence, vertical oscillation, or vertical ratio values experience marked differences in internal forces at the Achilles tendon and patellofemoral joint. Of these gait metrics, cadence is the most practical for out-of-lab use because of its ease of accurate measurement with consumer-grade devices.

This study presents the design and preliminary bench evaluation of a sensor-integrated prosthetic-leg prototype. The platform combines a multi-material PAHT-CF/TPU 95A foot, articulated knee and ankle mechanisms, two surface electromyography channels, an MPU6050 inertial measurement unit, an Arduino Uno controller, and MG995 servomotors. EMG threshold crossings select discrete knee-servomotor commands, while an accelerometer-derived inclination estimate selects between two ankle-servomotor commands. The evaluation comprised exploratory finite-element analyses, separate static compression tests, and qualitative demonstrations of the sensor-to-actuator pathways. The foot model predicted a maximum displacement of 25.96 mm under 400 N, whereas a separate compression test recorded approximately 7 mm at 1000 N; these values do not constitute quantitative model validation because the loading, constraints, and displacement measures differed. The shank model produced a maximum equivalent stress of 23.89 MPa, and a separate shank-knee assembly test reached approximately 1.85 kN. The foot-ankle connection produced a stress estimate of 203.6 MPa against an assumed strength value of 60 MPa, identifying a critical design limitation. Functional observations demonstrated sensor-triggered command execution, but joint tracking accuracy, response time, actuator output under load, and control repeatability were not quantified. The prototype therefore provides an initial laboratory platform for investigating mechanical and sensing integration; structural redesign and quantitative bench testing are required before any load-bearing or clinical use can be considered.

Background/Objectives: Acute insertional Achilles tendon rupture (A-IATR) is a rare, often season-ending injury in athletes. Revision after a failed repair is particularly challenging, and return to sport (RTS) after such surgery is rarely documented. We report one such case. MRI showed complete detachment with 15 mm of retraction and no residual tendon on the footprint. A single-stage procedure combining endoscopic double-row (SpeedBridge™) reinsertion and flexor hallucis longus (FHL) transfer was performed, followed by six weeks of non-weight-bearing cast immobilization and criteria-based rehabilitation, with Ankle-GO™-guided return to play. Return to play was authorized at 8.2 months (Ankle-GO™ 16/25); the patient returned to official competition at 9.4 months and was still competing approximately 17 months after surgery. At 15 months, the Achilles Tendon Total Rupture Score was 84 and the AOFAS score 90. No complication occurred. Conclusions: To our knowledge, this is the first report of RTS after this combined endoscopic revision technique. This single case suggests that this approach may be a feasible revision option in high-demand athletes; comparative studies are needed.

This prospective cohort study followed 161 collegiate athletes for one competitive season, integrating Functional Movement Screen task-level scores with wearable inertial measurement unit-derived features - including peak tibial acceleration asymmetry, surrogate vertical loading rate, and pelvis-trunk stability indices - within an explainable machine learning framework. Biomechanical features added an independent AUC increment of 0.07 beyond previous-injury history. SHAP analysis identified an interaction between tibial impact asymmetry and in-line lunge score that met the pre-specified directional stability criterion. Lateral ankle sprains commonly occur during directional changes and often lead to chronic ankle instability (CAI) associated with altered movement patterns, muscle weakness and atrophy. This study aimed to compare foot joint biomechanics during cutting among individuals with CAI, copers, and uninjured controls and to explore the relationship between intrinsic foot muscle sizes and functional status. Ankle and foot joint kinematics and kinetics were assessed using a multi-segment foot model during 45° side-step cutting at a mean approach speed of 3.5 m·s-1. Groups were compared using ANOVA or Kruskal-Wallis tests, and continuous biomechanical data were analysed using statistical parametric or non-parametric mapping. Cross-sectional area and thickness of the abductor hallucis and flexor digitorum brevis were recorded using ultrasound imaging. Muscle sizes were explored using general linear models, and correlations with questionnaire scores and physical examination outcomes were calculated. Foot joint kinematics and kinetics did not significantly differ between the groups. Individuals with CAI exhibited lower peak posterior ground reaction force than controls (mean difference: -6.2% of body weight, 95% CI: -11.9 to -0.4, p = 0.03). Quantitative sensory testing studies demonstrate that vibration perception, thermal detection, and sudomotor function deteriorate before patients report numbness or pain, suggesting a subclinical window of one to two chemotherapy cycles. I propose a phased prospective validation framework; specific monitoring recommendations should be regarded as hypotheses for testing rather than current clinical guidance. entry.title: The evidence landscape, clinical role, and mechanisms of action of robot-assisted injury treatment: a systematic review.
entry.content:
Ling X, Yin H · J Robot Surg · 2026

Robotic systems now appear at several points in injury care, but surgical navigation, fracture reduction, and neurorehabilitation are still reviewed largely within separate disciplines. This separation obscures how technical performance alters treatment delivery and whether those changes reach patient outcomes. We therefore mapped robotic applications across the injury-care pathway and examined the links among technological capability, treatment process, proximal mechanism, clinical outcome, and implementation context. We systematically searched the Web of Science Core Collection and Scopus for Articles and Reviews published from 1 January 2015 to 22 August 2026. The search retrieved 17,374 records (Scopus 10,584; WoSCC 6,790). A four-stage Python 3.12.14 deduplication audit reduced these to 12,304 unique records, after which publication-type restriction and title/abstract screening yielded 214 records (149 primary studies and 65 focused reviews/meta-analyses). Descriptive bibliometrics, structured coding with second-reviewer verification, and framework synthesis were used to map publication patterns, injury categories, robot roles, study designs, and proposed mechanism pathways. Among the 214 records, 151 (70.6%) were published during 2022-2026. The 32 records assigned to 2026 cover only the period through 22 August and were treated as a partial-year count. Most records concerned spinal cord injury (97 records) or fracture and orthopaedic trauma (95 records). Lower-limb or gait rehabilitation (93 records) and surgery or navigation (90 records) were the most frequent robot roles. The two pathways acted through different proximal processes: rehabilitation robots could modify training dose, assistance, and sensorimotor engagement, whereas surgical systems could modify localization, trajectory control, and execution error. Together, the studies described a clinical continuum, but evidence remained limited for patient-important outcomes, long-term follow-up, economic value, implementation conditions, and comparisons across platforms. Robotics research now extends from acute injury repair to longer-term functional reconstruction, although the link between technical performance and clinically meaningful benefit remains incompletely tested. The proposed framework follows this link across five levels: technological capability, treatment process, proximal mechanism, clinical outcome, and implementation context. It also sets out a research sequence from consistent terminology to scalable clinical use. Because clinical roles and study designs were classified from bibliographic records and title or abstract information, these findings describe the evidence landscape rather than indication-specific effectiveness. No pooled effect estimate or graded clinical recommendation was produced.

entry.title: Navicular fractures in elite athletes: Clarifying the evidence base of the 2025 International Foot and Ankle Sports Consensus.

Zimmermann FJ, Amling M, Simon A · Knee Surg Sports Traumatol Arthrosc · 2026

The recent international foot and ankle sports consensus and systematic review on navicular fractures in elite athletes addresses a highly relevant and challenging topic in sports medicine and provides valuable guidance in an area where standardized treatment and return to sport (RTS) recommendations remain limited. However, several methodological and reporting issues within the systematic review warrant clarification, given their potential influence on RTS decision-making. The reported mean RTS time of 8.2 weeks after operative treatment of navicular stress fractures appears to result from an error in the extraction of time units. Recalculation based on the included studies, after converting all values to weeks, yields a mean RTS of approximately 19.7 weeks (4.5 months), consistent with the expert consensus recommendation of 4-6 months after surgery. Further discrepancies concern the application of the stated eligibility criteria: 5 of the 14 included studies were published outside the specified 15-year window, and at least four involved cohorts with a mean age below 18 years despite paediatric studies being listed as an exclusion criterion. Further inconsistencies in study classification and reporting add to these concerns. We believe that clarification of these concerns is essential to ensure the reliability of the evidence base informing the consensus recommendations and to support accurate guidance for RTS decision-making in elite athletes with navicular fractures. entry.title: Detection of previous knee injuries using lower limb-worn inertial measurement units: A cross-sectional machine-learning study.
entry.content:
Valle C, Cotic M, Bartelt M, Seeberger L, et al. · Knee Surg Sports Traumatol Arthrosc · 2026

Previous knee injury increases the risk of subsequent injury, even after functional recovery, yet residual gait, running or load alterations often go undetected in routine assessment. Wearable inertial measurement units (IMUs) may enable scalable detection of such alterations outside laboratory settings. The primary aim of this study was to determine whether IMU-derived gait and running features can distinguish physically active individuals with a history of knee injury from uninjured controls using machine learning. In this cross-sectional study, 108 sports science students completed injury-history questionnaires and a walking-running-walking protocol on a 400 m track while wearing four IMUs. Of 90 participants with complete data, 23 reported prior knee injury and 67 were uninjured controls. Left- and right-side sensor data were combined into one per-participant feature vector. The model classified any prior knee injury (yes/no), not limb-specific injury. From 220 candidate features covering baseline gait, post-run changes, walk-to-run transitions, inter-limb asymmetry, variability and composite indices-a fixed pipeline (e.g., median imputation, mutual-information selection) was applied within leave-one-out cross-validation (primary) and repeated stratified five-fold cross-validation (secondary). Leave-one-out cross-validation correctly classified 76/90 participants (65/67 true negatives, 11/23 true positives), yielding an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve of 0.74, balanced accuracy of 0.72, sensitivity of 0.48, specificity of 0.97, positive predictive value (PPV) of 0.85 and negative predictive value of 0.84. Five-fold cross-validation produced more variable estimates, indicating substantial model instability across resampling partitions. As a proof of concept, IMU-derived features distinguished individuals with previous knee injury at high specificity but limited sensitivity. High specificity and PPV depend on the classification threshold and injury prevalence in this selected sample, not intrinsic model properties. Because predictors were not aligned to the injured side, findings cannot be interpreted biomechanically. Potential applications (e.g., targeted monitoring) require prospective external validation. Level II.

entry.title: The gait stability characteristics of individuals with chronic ankle instability.
entry.content:
Chen H, Kang Q, Yao M, Li D, et al. · Acta Orthop Traumatol Turc · 2026

The objective of this study was to investigate gait stability characteristics in patients with chronic ankle instability (CAI) by analyzing six degrees of freedom (6DOF) kinematic alterations in comparison with healthy controls. A cross-sectional study was conducted to evaluate 6DOF ankle kinematics in individuals with CAI and healthy controls using a dual fluoroscopic imaging system during treadmill walking. Three representative gait cycles were selected for each participant, normalized to 0-100% of the gait cycle, and averaged for analysis. Time-series kinematic differences were assessed using Statistical Parametric Mapping (SPM1D) with one-way ANOVA and post-hoc tests, while discrete variables were compared between groups with Bonferroniadjusted significance. Compared with the control group, the contralateral limbs demonstrated greater distal displacement during 44-55% of the gait cycle (2.7-3.8 mm, p<0.001), whereas the CAI limbs exhibited reduced plantarflexion during 68-75% of the gait cycle (5.1-7.3, p<0.001). Additionally, the range of motion (ROM) for abduction-adduction (2.5Åã, p<0.05) and internal-external rotation (2.4, p<0.05) on the CAI sides was smaller compared with the contralateral sides. Both the CAI and contralateral limbs showed a decrease in medial-lateral displacement in the coronal plane relative to the control group (3.1mm, p<.05). This study demostrated that individuals with CAI exhibit distinct gait strategies compared to healthy controls, characterized by a reduction in plantarflexion in the CAI sides, an increase in distal displacement in the contralateral sides, and an overall decrease in the ROM on the CAI sides.   Cite this article as: Chen H, Kang Q, Yao M, et al. entry.title: Correlation analysis between ankle proprioception and biomechanical characteristics in patients with chronic ankle instability.
entry.content:
Guo P, Wang J · Acta Bioeng Biomech · 2026

To compare ankle proprioception and biomechanical features between individuals with chronic ankle instability (CAI) and healthy controls, and to investigate the interplay between proprioceptive deficits and biomechanical alterations in CAI. Thirty-six male participants (18 CAI, 18 healthy controls) were recruited. Proprioception was evaluated using a joint position reproduction test, quantifying absolute errors. For biomechanical assessment, participants performed six single-leg hopping tests. An infrared motion-capture system (Vicon T40, 200 Hz) and a force platform (Kistler, 1,000 Hz) simultaneously captured ankle kinematics/kinetics. Ankle muscle activation was recorded via surface electromyography (Noraxon, 2,000 Hz). Participants with CAI demonstrated significantly greater joint position sense errors in plantarflexion (P = 0.002), dorsiflexion (P = 0.001), inversion (P = 0.011), and eversion (P = 0.022) compared with controls. Compared with healthy controls, individuals with CAI exhibited greater peak ankle inversion angles (P = 0.039), reduced peak ankle dorsiflexion angles (P = 0.029), and lower activation of the tibialis anterior (P = 0.019) and peroneus longus (P = 0.033) during single-leg landing. Correlation analyses indicated significant associations between inversion position sense errors and both peak ankle dorsiflexion angle (r = -0.584, P = 0.011) and peak ankle inversion angle (r = -0.622, P = 0.006) in the CAI group. Individuals with CAI exhibit impaired ankle proprioception and altered biomechanical characteristics compared with healthy controls. Decreased proprioception in the ankle was correlated with biomechanical defects. These findings suggest that proprioceptive impairments may contribute to persistent biomechanical abnormalities in CAI. Comprehensive interventions targeting proprioceptive enhancement may improve ankle biomechanics in this population.

entry.title: Design and biomechanical investigation of a patient-specific total talar prosthesis for total talar replacement: A finite element analysis.
entry.content:
Tabrej MQ, Kumar A, Biswas JK · Int J Artif Organs · 2026

Total talar replacement (TTR) is an emerging treatment for end-stage talar diseases, although concerns persist regarding ankle stability due to essential ligament transection. Further investigation is necessary regarding the biomechanical impact of patient-specific total talar prosthesis (TTP) on ankle stability and bone-implant mechanics. The purpose of this study is designing a patient-specific TTP and assess its biomechanical performance on ankle stability and stress distribution under various loading conditions using finite element analysis. A CT scan is used to create a 3D finite element model of the foot and ankle complex. The TTP made of A dual-material (UHMWPE talar body and titanium alloy cage) was created and fixed with five screws. Four loading conditions were simulated: inversion, eversion, dorsiflexion, and plantarflexion, with forces of 10 N, 50 N, 100 N, and 150 N. Talar tilt angles and von Mises stresses were examined for intact and implanted models. In comparison to the intact ankle, TTR significantly decreased the talar tilt angles in inversion (12.5%-16%), eversion (6.6%-14%), and dorsiflexion (33%-47%). On the other hand, plantarflexion produced a larger tilt (34%-44%). While bone stresses stayed below 5 MPa, maximum implant stresses ranged from 20 to 80 MPa. The validation of the model against cadaveric studies was reliable. The patient-specific TTP with screw fixation improves ankle stability in most loading directions, potentially compensating for ligament insufficiency. However, greater plantarflexion instability necessitates post-operative measures. These findings provide biomechanical evidence that fixation-enhanced TTP designs can improve therapeutic outcomes.

entry.title: Plate-Based Operative Management of Medial Malleolar Stress Fractures in High-Level Basketball Players: A Short Report.
entry.content:
O'Malley E, Kim J, O'Malley M · Foot Ankle Int · 2026

Medial malleolar stress fractures (MMSFs) are uncommon but potentially high-risk injuries in athletes. In basketball players, repetitive jumping, landing, and cutting may expose the characteristic vertical fracture pattern to substantial shear, yet sport-specific operative data remain limited. This study reports the outcomes of plate-based fixation for MMSFs in high-level basketball players. A retrospective case series was performed of 10 high-level basketball players treated surgically for MMSF between 2007 and 2025. All patients underwent radiography, magnetic resonance imaging, and computed tomography (CT). Operative treatment consisted of shear resisting plate-based fixation (one-third tubular anti-glide or hook plate) with fracture-perpendicular screws, selective bone grafting, biologic augmentation, and treatment of associated anterior impingement when indicated. Primary outcomes were radiographic union, return to play, and need for additional surgery. All patients were male, with a median age of 20.5 years (range, 18-26). Median height was 205.5 cm (IQR, 198-213), and the median weight was 103.5 kg (IQR, 93-113). Eight players were professional and 2 were collegiate athletes later drafted professionally. CT demonstrated a vertically oriented fracture arising from the anteromedial tibial plafond in all cases. Union was achieved in all players. Nine returned to full team activities by 12 weeks and to competitive play at a median of 4 months (range, 3-4 months). One player sustained a traumatic refracture 8 months after index fixation, required 2 revision procedures, ultimately healed after supplemental anterior plating, and returned to play at 6 months. Plate-based fixation was associated with reliable union and return to play, although revision surgery was required in 1 of 10 players. Given the consistent vertical fracture morphology and substantial sport-specific loading demands, shear resisting plating may be considered in this population. Level IV, case series.

entry.title: Unilateral Exoskeleton Training for Balance/Gait in Hemiplegic Stroke: Pilot Study.
entry.content:
Zhou S, Wang S, Qu X, Fan J, et al. · Behav Neurol · 2026

The aim of this study is to evaluate the effects of a unilateral-lower limb exoskeleton rehabilitation training robot on balance and lower limb function after stroke. In this pilot study, stroke patients with hemiplegic at Tongji University Yangzhi Rehabilitation Hospital (between October 2022 and December 2023) were randomly assigned to either the robot group or the control group. The primary measure was the Berg balance scale (BBS), whereas secondary measures included the 10-m walking time test, 6-min walk test, three-dimensional gait analysis, and pain levels using the Hospital Anxiety and Depression Scale (HADS) and visual analogue scale (VAS). Among 36 post-stroke hemiplegia patients (25 males; 18 per group), the robot group significantly outperformed the traditional group. The robot group improved BBS scores (5.50 ± 2.09 vs. 3.11 ± 1.50, p < 0.001), 6-min walking distance (15.89 ± 8.64 m vs. 9.73 ± 5.83 m, p = 0.017), and 10-m walking time reduction (8.82 ± 3.22 s vs. 6.83 ± 1.81 s, p = 0.030). Gait parameters also showed greater gains: hip flexion (3.57°±2.30° vs. 1.72°±2.15°, p = 0.018), knee flexion (5.28°±4.89° vs. 2.63°±2.37°, p = 0.046), and ankle dorsiflexion (4.81°±5.57° vs. 1.09°±4.19°, p = 0.030). Depression scores improved more in the robot group (2.89 ± 1.75 vs. 1.61 ± 1.20, p = 0.015). No significant differences occurred in anxiety or pain VAS scores (p > 0.05). Integrating a unilateral-lower limb exoskeleton rehabilitation robot with traditional therapy significantly enhances lower limb recovery in stroke patients with hemiplegia. Future large-scale randomized controlled trials and follow-up evaluations are needed to validate the current findings.

entry.title: Exposure-adjusted injury incidence and the impact of surveillance definitions in handball: a systematic review and meta-analysis of prospective cohort studies.
entry.content:
Naderi A, Shaabani F, Alghosi M, Wedderkopp N, et al. · Res Sports Med · 2026

Handball carries a substantial injury burden, though reported incidence varies. This systematic review and meta-analysis quantified exposure-adjusted injury incidence in handball by synthesizing prospective cohort studies. Sixteen studies (11,049 players) were included. The pooled overall injury incidence was 5.05 per 1,000 hours; however, substantial heterogeneity was observed and prediction intervals were wide. Match incidence was significantly higher than training incidence, and contact injuries exceeded non-contact injuries. Notably, the difference between non-time-loss and time-loss injuries was not statistically significant (p = 0.058). Back players had significantly higher match injury rates than goalkeepers, and elite players exceeded amateurs. The knee and ankle were the most frequently injured anatomical locations, predominantly sustaining contusions and sprains. These findings emphasize the need for standardized surveillance and targeted prevention for match-related contact injuries, while highlighting that pooled rates require cautious interpretation due to extreme between-study variability.

entry.title: Metatarsal Strains During Loading and Motion of the Foot and Ankle in a Cadaveric Model.
entry.content:
Nicolescu JM, Le AH, Peterson AC, Rodriguez R, et al. · J Orthop Res · 2026

Metatarsal bone stress injuries (BSI) are painful, overuse injuries commonly seen in athletes and military personnel. High strain magnitudes combined with repetitive loading cycles causes bone fatigue and microdamage accumulation. To protect against BSI, it is necessary to determine how to limit bone strain magnitude without sacrificing physical activity. This study examined maximum and minimum principal dorsal strains of metatarsals 2-4 during tibial dorsiflexion/plantarflexion, external/internal rotation, and varus/valgus alignment with four underfoot conditions. Five lower-limb cadaveric specimens were instrumented with strain gauges on metatarsals 2-4 and a robotic actuator applied 25% bodyweight and moved the ankle/foot through its envelope of passive motion. Dorsiflexion and varus tibial motion produced the greatest increase in strain magnitudes during all underfoot conditions. Adding half-inch blocks beneath the medial and lateral forefoot caused principal strain magnitudes to increase threefold within the metatarsals adjacent to the block across all motions. Passive engagement of the windlass mechanism during dorsiflexion caused approximately a threefold increase in maximum principal strain of metatarsals 2-3 coinciding with a significant decrease in metatarsal 4. The results emphasize the role that the arch and its supporting structures play in modulating metatarsal loading even within a passive model.

entry.title: Balance Wood, a Bilateral Ankle-Controlled Serious Game for Healthy Adults: 2-Stage Cross-Sectional Development and Usability Study.
entry.content:
Zhang Y, Yamamoto J, Han T, Song Q, et al. · JMIR Serious Games · 2026

Ankle mobility and control contribute to balance and everyday movement throughout adulthood, yet are usually assessed through repetitive, abstract tasks that reveal little about movement production. Serious games can make repeated tasks engaging, but most report only end point scores rather than continuous gameplay signals, and few establish system usability. Developing and evaluating such a system in healthy adults is a necessary first step. This study aimed to develop Balance Wood, a bilateral ankle-controlled serious game in which seated players tilt a device through ankle flexion-extension to control on-screen play, to describe the system and the signals it records, and to evaluate its usability, safety, and user experience in healthy adults. In this two-stage cross-sectional development and usability study, healthy adults without lower-limb injury or balance-affecting neurological or vestibular disorders completed single-session repeated-measures procedures. In stage 1, a total of 40 adults-20 older (mean age 73.0, SD 5.9 y; 10 women) and 20 younger (mean age 28.1, SD 3.2 y; 4 women) adults-completed 3 fixed-order difficulty levels in 1 session (exploratory signal analysis). In stage 2, a total of 18 younger adults (mean age 24.6, SD 3.9 y; 5 women) completed the levels in counterbalanced order. Usability was assessed with the System Usability Scale (0-100); use impressions and consciously used body parts with Likert and open-ended items; and device tilt-angle accuracy against a digital goniometer. The mean System Usability Scale score was 81.5 (SD 11.2; 95% CI 76.0-87.1; Cronbach α=.74), above the benchmark of 68, indicating good perceived usability. Mean ratings were 2.11 (SD 1.32) for safety concern (95% CI 1.45-2.77) and 1.67 (SD 1.03) for pain (95% CI 1.15-2.18). Ankle use was highest at 4.94 (SD 0.24), exceeding knee 2.50 (SD 1.29), hip 2.00 (SD 1.24), and trunk 2.17 (SD 1.15) by Wilcoxon signed-rank tests (P<.001). Device readings agreed closely with the goniometer, with a mean absolute error of 0.66°, an intraclass correlation coefficient of 0.999, and 95% limits of agreement of -0.68 to 1.70°. In stage 1, all measures were computable for the 40 participants, with typical amplitudes of 20.5° to 27.2° and stable speed in both groups. In stage 2, repeated-measures analyses (α=.05) did not detect statistically significant differences across difficulty conditions or presentation positions (all P>.13). In healthy adults, Balance Wood was usable, well-accepted, low-risk, and provided accurate device-level tilt measurement with predominantly ankle-based control while continuously recording gameplay signals. It is a low-cost, bilateral, ankle-specific control interface with continuous signal capture into 1 easy-to-use device. Its contribution is a reproducible, usability-tested platform with characterized device accuracy, and formally defined candidate measures awaiting validation. Once validated, it could support home- or community-based recording; in the near term, it is a research tool.

entry.title: Long-Term Injury Patterns and Trends in Elite Professional Football: A Nine-Season Retrospective Analysis of Prospectively Recorded Data.
entry.content:
Bandalović A, Veršić Š, Škomrlj J, Pranjić T, et al. · Life (Basel) · 2026

Long-term injury surveillance in professional football is essential for understanding temporal changes in injury patterns. However, prospective studies spanning multiple consecutive seasons within the same professional club remain scarce. This study aimed to investigate injury epidemiology, temporal trends, and injury characteristics over nine consecutive seasons in an elite Croatian professional football club. This retrospective longitudinal study over nine competitive seasons (2015/16-2023/24) included 167 male players participating in the professional first-team environment from a single professional football club, contributing a total of 382 player-seasons across nine consecutive seasons. A total of 749 time-loss injuries were recorded according to the FIFA Medical Assessment and Research Centre (F-MARC) consensus recommendations. Temporal trends were evaluated using Joinpoint regression, while injury characteristics, anatomical distribution, tissue involvement, and injury burden were analysed descriptively. Overall injury incidence averaged 12.66 injuries per 1000 h of exposure (95% CI: 11.77-13.60), with substantially higher incidence during matches (50.13 injuries/1000 h) than training (7.97 injuries/1000 h). Joinpoint regression identified a non-significant annual decline in injury incidence before the COVID-19 season (2019/2020) (APC = -9.66%), followed by a non-significant increase thereafter (APC = 4.88%). At least one injury was recorded in 295 player-seasons, corresponding to 77.2% of all eligible player-seasons. More than 80% of all injuries involved the lower extremities, while muscle injuries accounted for almost half of all recorded injuries. Functional muscle disorders were the most frequent injury type, whereas meniscal and articular cartilage injuries were associated with the highest mean time loss per injury. The predominance of lower-limb muscle injuries, together with the substantial burden associated with less frequent intra-articular knee injuries, highlights key priorities for injury prevention in professional football. Long-term surveillance within the same club provides valuable insights into evolving injury patterns and supports the development of targeted strategies to maximise player availability.
